page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Entropy statement
lines: In every spontaneous process, the total
steps.why: The entropy form is the one the rest of the chapter uses: it turns spontaneity into a measurable test. It earns the first of the two marks; the heat flow statement in the next step earns the second, so a full-mark answer carries both.
common_mistakes: Writing that the entropy of the system alone always increases — the system's entropy can fall while the total still rises.
steps.memory_tip: Second law: total entropy rises. Count the system and the surroundings together.
steps.margin_note: The word total (or universe) must appear.

steps.label: Heat flow statement
steps.mark_note: Heat flow statement — the second of the 2 marks
lines: Equivalent statement: heat cannot flow on
its own from a colder body to a hotter

lines.text: Total entropy increases in every spontaneous process

steps.why: Both statements describe the same physics: natural change runs in the direction of rising total entropy, and cold-to-hot heat flow would lower it. The mark split gives 1 mark to each statement, so writing only one of them earns 1 mark out of 2, not full marks.
common_mistakes: Reversing the direction — heat flows on its own from hot to cold, never from cold to hot.
steps.memory_tip: On its own, heat goes hot to cold. The reverse needs outside work, as in a refrigerator.
steps.margin_note: The book prints both forms. Write both — each one carries a mark.

insider_note: Two equivalent statements exist and the printed answer gives both, joined by or. This card scores them one mark each: the entropy statement earns 1 mark and the heat flow statement earns the other. Writing only one of them earns 1 mark out of 2, so write both — the second statement costs one extra line.
